topic: Cardiff Pact and UK Federal Challenge

subtopics.title: Devolution and the asymmetric UK framework
subtopics.summary: Devolution transfers powers from the central government to subnational institutions, while the centre keeps ultimate constitutional authority. In the UK, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved institutions, but the extent and nature of their powers differ, so the arrangement is asymmetric rather than uniform. The UK Treasury uses the Barnett Formula to set changes in block grant funding for these administrations.
facts: Devolution means transfer of powers from central government to subnational institutions
Ultimate constitutional authority is retained at the centre
Devolved institutions in the UK: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Extent and nature of devolved powers differ among the three
UK devolution is asymmetric rather than uniform
Scotland Act 1998 established the Scottish Parliament and devolved substantial domestic powers
Government of Wales Act 1998 established the Welsh Legislature, now known as the Senedd
Barnett Formula is used by the UK Treasury to set block grant changes
UK Internal Market Act 2020 regulates the domestic UK market after Brexit
Devolved governments criticised the 2020 Act as reducing their regulatory autonomy

subtopics.title: Historical formation of the Union
subtopics.summary: The UK's constituent nations joined the union at different points. Wales was incorporated into the English legal and political system through the Act of Union of 1536, while later Acts of Union brought Scotland (1707) and Ireland (1801) into the state. After most of Ireland became independent in 1922, six counties remained within the UK as Northern Ireland.
facts: Wales was incorporated into the English legal and political system; Act of Union in 1536

subtopics.title: Good Friday Agreement and Northern Ireland
subtopics.summary: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement, signed on 10 April 1998, ended the conflict known as The Troubles in Northern Ireland. It set up power-sharing government, allowed reunification with Ireland subject to a referendum, and let citizens hold Irish or British nationality or both. After the 2022 deadlock over government formation, a new deal was published as the command paper Safeguarding the Union.

subtopics.title: Cardiff Pact and the UK federal challenge
subtopics.summary: The Cardiff Pact is a political Memorandum of Understanding signed in Cardiff by leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and it is not a legally binding treaty. It asks Westminster to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change and affirms each nation's right to hold independence referendums. The UK government rejects new referendums, relying on a 2022 Supreme Court ruling that the Scottish Parliament cannot legislate for one without Westminster's consent.
facts: Cardiff Pact is an inter-party accord signed in Cardiff (Wales)
Signatories include John Swinney (SNP), Rhun ap Iorwerth (Plaid Cymru) and Michelle O'Neill (Sinn Fein Vice President)
Mary Lou McDonald (Sinn Fein President) also attended
The pact is a political Memorandum of Understanding, not a legally binding treaty
Core objectives: prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change; affirm right to hold independence referendums; coordinate policies on economy, energy and European relations
Scotland and Wales would seek EU membership as new states
Northern Ireland would rejoin the EU through unification with the Republic of Ireland
All three devolved administrations are now led by pro-independence parties
UK government rejects new independence referendums without appropriate constitutional and legal authority
2022 UK Supreme Court ruling (Reference by the Lord Advocate): Scottish Parliament cannot unilaterally legislate for an independence referendum without Westminster's consent

quizzes.passage: Political leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland signed a Memorandum of Understanding in Cardiff, asserting the principle of self-determination and calling for constitutional changes within the United Kingdom. The move has renewed debate over the UK's devolution framework, under which power is transferred from the central government to subnational institutions while ultimate constitutional authority stays at the centre. Devolution in the UK is asymmetric, because the extent and nature of devolved powers differ among the territories. The pact is a political understanding rather than a legally binding treaty. It asks Westminster to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change, and it affirms each nation's right to hold independence referendums. The UK government has rejected demands for new independence referendums, saying such votes need appropriate constitutional and legal authority. In the 2016 Brexit referendum, Scotland and Northern Ireland both voted to remain in the EU, which fed into these debates. Scotland and Wales would seek EU membership as new states, while Northern Ireland would rejoin the EU through unification with the Republic of Ireland. The pact is seen as the most coordinated challenge to the UK's union structure since the Good Friday Agreement.

quizzes.passage: The United Kingdom was built in stages, and its constituent nations joined it at different times. Wales was brought into the English legal and political system through an Act of Union passed in the sixteenth century. The English and Scottish parliaments were united in 1707, creating a single new state. Ireland joined later, when another Act of Union brought it into the United Kingdom. Most of Ireland became independent after an Anglo-Irish War, while six counties in the north remained within the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland now each have devolved institutions, but the extent of their powers differs. Scotland's Parliament and Wales's legislature were set up by separate Acts of Parliament, and Westminster retains ultimate constitutional authority over all of these arrangements. After Brexit, Northern Ireland came to share a land border with an EU member state. New checks were then introduced between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and these checks angered Unionists who believed they undermined Northern Ireland's position within the UK. This layered history explains why devolution differs across the nations, and why these tensions continue to shape political debate.
